name: Action for Happiness: wellbeing courses and digital programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build, weighted by branch result: the courses and groups (about a tenth) mostly in the UK (343 of the first 431 courses, Krekel et al. 2021), and the digital programme (nine-tenths), an English-language online audience, judged at 40% UK, 25% US, 6% each Canada and Australia, 3% Ireland and 20% elsewhere.
summary: Action for Happiness, a UK charity, spent £551,000 in 2025 on 160 volunteer-led Happiness Habits wellbeing courses (about 1,900 people), 115 volunteer-led local groups, and a digital programme (calendars of daily actions, an app, the 10 Days of Happiness emails and live talks) through which it says 190,000 people took at least one wellbeing action. The courses' effect blends the randomised trial of their predecessor, Exploring What Matters (life satisfaction up 0.63 standard deviations, about a point), with the literature on group positive psychology courses; the digital programme takes the literature on self-help exercises for the share of people judged to use a programme like the trials' (15%). The digital programme's reach is an audience built since 2011 and served at mostly fixed cost, so its result is a past average and counts at the charity's next-dollar figure (44%); the courses are priced per course. It comes to about 0.14 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.02-1.0), nearly nine-tenths of it from the digital programme. Every branch is discounted for missing data (no trial of today's six-week course, the local groups or the digital programmes); the biggest uncertainties are how many of the 190,000 get anything like a programme and how long the effects last.

rows.label: Exploring What Matters trial: effect on life satisfaction (SD)

source.title: Krekel, De Neve, Fancourt and Layard 2021, supplementary materials
source.page: Table 2a, column 1 (life satisfaction), Treatment*Post with controls

rows.explainer: The randomised trial of the charity's eight-week course: 146 participants of six London courses (2016-2017), randomised to the course or a wait-list two months later; life satisfaction (0-10) rose 0.633 standard deviations of the control group (SE 0.152, so 95% CI 0.335-0.931), about one point. The effect without controls is 0.64 (Figure 3). Measured before the last session, against a wait-list whose scores did not change.

rows.explainer: The prior: the meta-analysis's subgroup of group-delivered positive psychology interventions, 0.38 SD on subjective wellbeing (5 trials, 95% CI 0.03-0.73), the closest reference class to a facilitated group course. All 28 trials pool to 0.34 (0.22-0.45), and the group, individual and self-help subgroups don't differ (p = 0.91). No prediction interval is published; its spread is built in the standard error below.

rows.explainer: Inverse-variance weight of the trial against the prior: about 76%.

rows.label: Trial's relevance to today's course (multiplies its weight)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5-1). The trial tested Exploring What Matters, eight in-person weekly sessions of 2-2.5 hours in London; today's Happiness Habits keeps its structure (Tune In, Connect, Take Action) and volunteer pairs but runs six two-hour sessions, mostly online, with revised content. A shorter, partly online version of the same course is close, but not the course trialled. Anchor: the precision weight itself; at 0.5 the trial still counts a little more than the literature.

rows.label: Trial's weight in the blend
rows.explainer: About 61%.

rows.label: Course: effect at the end of the course (SD)
rows.explainer: The trial and the literature blended by weight: about 0.53 SD of life satisfaction.

rows.label: Course: years until the effect has faded

source.title: Bolier, Haverman, Westerhof, Riper, Smit and Bohlmeijer 2013, Positive psychology interventions: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled studies, BMC Public Health 13:119
source.page: Results, follow-up

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 1 year (0.5-2.5), with a linear fade. The meta-analysis's six trials with 3-6 month follow-ups keep 0.22 of 0.34 SD (about 65% at four and a half months), which a linear fade to zero reaches at about 1.1 years. The trial found the effect undiminished two months after the course (exploratory, no control group by then; Krekel et al. 2021, p. 25), which allows longer; the meta-analysis pools follow-ups only to six months (a few of its trials ran to a year).

rows.label: Digital: effect of a self-help positive psychology programme (SD)

source.title: Bolier, Haverman, Westerhof, Riper, Smit and Bohlmeijer 2013, Positive psychology interventions: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled studies, BMC Public Health 13:119
source.page: Table 4, subjective well-being by type of intervention

rows.explainer: The meta-analysis's 20 trials of self-help positive psychology interventions (gratitude, kindness, savouring exercises, many online), 0.33 SD on subjective wellbeing (95% CI 0.20-0.46), for people who sign up for a programme like 10 Days of Happiness. No trial of the charity's own digital programmes is published. Exercises of four weeks or less do as well as longer ones (0.35, 17 trials).

rows.label: Digital: years until the effect has faded

source.title: Bolier, Haverman, Westerhof, Riper, Smit and Bohlmeijer 2013, Positive psychology interventions: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled studies, BMC Public Health 13:119
source.page: Results, follow-up

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 1 year (0.4-2), with a linear fade: the meta-analysis's pooled follow-ups (six trials, self-help and group among them) keep about 65% of the effect at four and a half months, which a linear fade reaches at about 1.1 years; post-test effects don't differ by delivery or length, so self-help takes the same anchor as the courses. Lower end: a few days of emails may fade faster than the weeks-long programmes the trials ran.

rows.label: Local groups: a year of monthly meetings against a course's effect
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10-70%): a local group meets about two hours a month (some 24 hours a year, against a course's 12 in six weeks) to talk over actions from the same material, but unstructured and with many attendees who have done the course already, whose gain is counted there. No study of the groups exists; the range is wide.

rows.label: Course and groups: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)

source.title: White, Uttl and Holder 2019, Meta-analyses of positive psychology interventions: the effects are much smaller than previously reported, PLoS ONE 14(5):e0216588
source.page: Results, re-analysis of Bolier et al. (2013), subjective well-being
source.quote: the limit meta-analyses (Fig 10, bottom panel) estimated an effect size of r = .13

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.65 (0.4-0.9), what the blend leaves out. Internal: an unblinded wait-list trial of self-selected participants, on a course sold as raising happiness, with self-reported outcomes (the biomarkers moved the right way but not significantly), and co-authored by the charity's co-founder and trustee; and a literature whose subjective-wellbeing effect shrinks when small-study bias is corrected (Bolier's set: r = 0.17 by random effects, 0.13 by limit meta-analysis, about 0.76 of it). About 0.7 together: 0.76 for small-study bias, a little more for the self-report and the co-author. External: today's participants are like the trial's (members choosing a course), but worldwide and online; about 0.95. After the blend and every adjustment the course counts about 0.21 of the trial's 0.63 SD (0.11 after the missing-data step). Anchor: charityevals' Refugee Council model takes 0.5 for small heterogeneous trials of therapy.

rows.label: Digital: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)

source.title: White, Uttl and Holder 2019, Meta-analyses of positive psychology interventions: the effects are much smaller than previously reported, PLoS ONE 14(5):e0216588
source.page: Results, re-analysis of Bolier et al. (2013), subjective well-being
source.quote: the limit meta-analyses (Fig 10, bottom panel) estimated an effect size of r = .13

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.6 (0.35-0.85). Internal: correcting Bolier's subjective-wellbeing trials for small-study bias keeps about 0.76 of the effect (r = 0.17 to 0.13); the self-help trials are small, unblinded and self-reported, with one high-quality trial near zero; about 0.7. External: the trials recruited people into a set programme with reminders; the charity's users pick up a calendar, an app or ten days of emails on their own; and most of the self-help trials measured positive affect rather than life satisfaction, which the shared rate then turns into life-satisfaction points; about 0.85 for both. That most of the 190,000 take a single action rather than a programme is the delivery adjustment's question, not this one. Anchor: the courses' 0.65, a little lower on external validity.

rows.label: Course and groups: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 95% (85-100%). The trial's effect is against a wait-list whose scores didn't change, so recovery and life as usual are netted out. A little below 1 for other wellbeing courses, apps and talking therapies (NHS Talking Therapies take self-referrals) that some participants would have turned to instead, which the wait-listed controls, waiting for this course, did not.

rows.label: Digital: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 90% (75-100%). The trials' effects are against controls (no programme or a placebo) who were free to use anything else, so self-help available then is netted out. Below 1 only for what has come since the trials of 2005-2012: free wellbeing and meditation apps, now widespread, that people who seek out a happiness calendar or app would likely use instead, which those controls mostly could not. Anchor: the courses' 95%, lower because an app is a closer substitute for an app than for a group course.

rows.label: Volunteer hours per course (both leaders)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 36 hours (26-70): two leaders each run six two-hour sessions (24 hours together) and prepare and follow up (about an hour a session each, 12 more). Their training is counted below.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 72 hours (36-120): two hosts at twelve monthly meetings, about three hours each with set-up.

rows.label: Value of the volunteers' time
rows.formula: (courses_delivered * volunteer_hours_per_course + local_groups * volunteer_hours_per_group + new_volunteers * volunteer_training_hours) * @united_kingdom.volunteer_hour_value_2025 * usd_per_gbp
rows.explainer: Hours at the site's 2025 UK value of a volunteer hour (@united_kingdom.volunteer_hour_value_2025, £17.96), in dollars: Convention 2 counts volunteers' unpaid time as others' resources.

rows.label: Course and groups: the charity's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The courses' and groups' spending over that plus the volunteers' time (leading, hosting and training): about 43%. Participants' donations are the charity's income, already in its cost; venues are mostly online or the leaders' own.

rows.label: Digital: the charity's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 95% (85-100%): the charity makes the calendars, app and programmes itself; guest speakers at its talks give their time, and partners (the Wellbeing Research Centre at Oxford for the International Day of Happiness campaign) share some campaigns.

rows.label: Course: delivery adjustment (fidelity)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 95% (80-100%), fidelity only: the trial's six courses ran in London under the researchers' eye; today's volunteer pairs follow a manual but may adapt it (the trial's authors note some adaptation is allowed). Attendance is not discounted: no dose-response is shown (Convention 5), and the trial's effect already includes its participants' missed sessions. Shorter content is in the trial's relevance weight, not here.

rows.label: Digital: share of people counted who get a programme like the trials'
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 15% (5-30%). The trials gave people a structured programme of exercises; of the 190,000 who took at least one action, 25,000 started 10 Days of Happiness that year and some app users follow its daily programme, while most took a single action from a calendar, a talk or a post, which no trial measures. Anchor: 25,000 of about 187,000 is 13%, plus regular app users, less 10 Days starters who drop out early (the trials' own attrition is in their effects).

rows.label: Course and groups: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the courses are counted (160) but their size is a judgment, the trial was of the earlier eight-week in-person course rather than today's six-week, mostly online Happiness Habits, and the local groups have no data at all. So the shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Digital: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: no evaluation of the charity's calendars, app or 10 Days of Happiness; the effect is the literature on self-help exercises and the share who use them is a judgment. So the shared missing-data step.

rows.label: Course and groups: side effects (leaders' own wellbeing, kindness to others)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +8% (-2 to +25%): the volunteer leaders (two per course, some 320 a year) likely gain as participants do, though they start happier; the course raised compassion and social trust by about half a standard deviation and acts of kindness, which benefit people outside the household. A small downside for anyone who delays needed treatment because they took a course instead.

rows.label: Digital: side effects (wider reach, campaigns, schools)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +5% (-5 to +20%): posts seen by millions who take no counted action, the schools resources and the International Day of Happiness campaign may shift a little wellbeing or policy attention, unmeasured; screen time and messages that leave the unhappy feeling worse are a small downside.

rows.label: Course and groups: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the course branch's adjustments; the local groups take the same ones.

rows.label: Digital: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the digital branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Course WELLBYs after adjustments (before side effects)
rows.explainer: Participants × WELLBYs each × household × adjustments.

rows.label: Local-group WELLBYs after adjustments (before side effects)
rows.explainer: Attendees × WELLBYs each × household × the courses' adjustments.

rows.label: Digital WELLBYs after adjustments (before side effects)
rows.explainer: People counted × WELLBYs per programme user × household × adjustments (the share who use a programme is in them).

rows.label: Courses' and groups' share of the WELLBYs
rows.explainer: Weight for the outcome-weighted averages below, for reading only.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, outcome-weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share that wouldn't have happened anyway, outcome-weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome: the outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

source.title: Krekel, De Neve, Fancourt and Layard 2021, A local community course that raises wellbeing and pro-sociality: evidence from a randomised controlled trial, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 188:322-336 (accepted manuscript)

rows.explainer: The trial's participants, the one published profile of the charity's course-takers; used for every branch.

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of the people reached
rows.explainer: The two rates weighted by the participants' sex: about 7.5 per 100,000.

rows.label: Share of participants with moderate or worse depression

source.title: Krekel, De Neve, Fancourt and Layard 2021, A local community course that raises wellbeing and pro-sociality: evidence from a randomised controlled trial, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 188:322-336 (accepted manuscript)
source.page: p. 12, Outcomes
source.quote: we found that 24 out of 133 respondents for whom we had data at t=1 (about 18%) showed medium or strong depressive symptomatology

rows.explainer: The trial's share with PHQ-9 of 10 or more, 18%; the range allows for app users and course-takers who differ from the London sample. Only their excess risk is counted.

rows.label: Relative risk of suicide with depression
rows.explainer: Judgment 5 (2-15), as charityevals' Refugee Council model: the meta-analysis of Harris and Barraclough (1997, British Journal of Psychiatry 170:205-228) puts the standardised mortality ratio for suicide in major depression at about 20; people with moderate symptoms in the community run lower (about 2-3), so 5 is a midpoint.

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of the people reached without depression
rows.explainer: The population rate already includes the depressed; this nets them out, so that the excess counted below is the depressed share's alone (as charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project model does).

rows.label: Course: share of the excess suicide risk removed at the end of the course
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (2-30%): the course lowered PHQ-9 by about half a standard deviation (Krekel et al. 2021, p. 17); the risk is taken to fall with part of the symptom change, as in charityevals' Refugee Council model (20% for therapy's larger effect on depression).

rows.label: Course: suicides averted per participant (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The site's recipe (templates.md, wellbeing), for the depressed share only: the excess risk falls with the effect and the deaths come over its years, discounted like the WELLBYs.

rows.label: Digital: suicides averted per programme user (before adjustments)
rows.formula: nondepressed_suicide_rate * depressed_share * (depression_suicide_rr - 1) * course_share_excess_removed * (digital_initial_effect_sd / course_initial_effect_sd) * 0.5 * digital_effect_duration_years * digital_discount_factor
rows.explainer: The same recipe with the share of risk removed scaled by the digital effect against the course's, over the digital effect's years.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments), average
rows.formula: (course_people * course_deaths_averted_per_person + group_people * course_deaths_averted_per_person * group_effect_ratio + digital_people * digital_deaths_averted_per_person) / people_reached
rows.explainer: People-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; the local groups at their effect ratio.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by age band, mixed by the ages of suicides in England and Wales (ONS, 2025: 53% at 15-49, 47% at 50 or older, valued at the 50-74 weight), times your value of a life. The participants' ages track the adult population's (Krekel et al. 2021, p. 8).

rows.label: Deaths averted, in units of value
rows.formula: ((course_people + group_people * group_effect_ratio) * course_deaths_averted_per_person * course_total_adj + digital_people * digital_deaths_averted_per_person * digital_total_adj * marginal_vs_past_average) * value_per_death
rows.explainer: Each branch's suicides averted after its own adjustments (the digital programme's at the next-dollar figure), valued the site's way.

rows.label: Deaths averted, in WELLBYs (cancelled by the unit's conversion)
rows.explainer: The one row that puts units of value into WELLBYs; the WELLBY unit's conversion multiplies it back, so the deaths count exactly their shared value at any WELLBY rate.

rows.label: WELLBYs
rows.formula: (course_wellbys + group_wellbys) * (1 + course_unmodelled_benefits_adj) + digital_wellbys * (1 + digital_unmodelled_benefits_adj) * marginal_vs_past_average + wellbys_from_uov
rows.explainer: The three branches with their side effects, the digital programme's at the next-dollar figure (its cost is a past average), plus the suicides averted.

rows.label: Digital: how much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: The digital programme's 2025 reach (190,000 people taking an action) comes from an audience built since 2011 (780,000 members, 76,000 of them new in 2025; 270,000 app users to date), served at mostly fixed cost; a year's spending over it is a past average, and the next dollar has to recruit new users or build the new platform. So the digital branch counts at the charity's own next-dollar figure (facts/next_dollar.json, normalization.md 2.10), applied in the outcome; the courses and groups are bought course by course at about their cost, so they don't take it. 1 in `published`: the past average itself.
